newsitem.title: UK: Dollar mixed, torn between US/Japan trade and EMU.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed, torn between US/Japan trade and EMU.

text.p: The dollar was mixed at European midsession as the market kept one eye on EMU and the other on the trade gap between the U.S. and Japan.

Dollar/mark took heart from expectations of a weak single currency, stoked by Monday's deal on the EU budget stability pact, though it was off highs by midday after a French minister stirred doubts over France's commitment to monetary union.

Dollar/yen shook off early weakness, though analysts said its upside would remain limited as the market focused on the ballooning U.S./Japan trade gap expected to be revealed in data due out tonight and on Thursday.
The dollar was quoted at 1.7348/53 marks at 1047 GMT, off a morning high of 1.7372, and at 113.63/78 yen -- well above its early low of 112.93.

French European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscivici gave a fillip to a broadly weaker mark when he said Paris would make the final decision on "whether or not to move to the euro" after assessing the state of its public finances.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said earlier that an audit of public finances should be ready by around July 14.
But the overall mark tone remained soft after the stability pact deal struck yesterday fed fears of a timely but weak euro.

"Overall people do think EMU will progress and that the chances are it will be a weak one -- that's a reason the dollar's fairly well underpinned," said Alan Collins, head of technical analysis at Merita Bank in London.

Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp's comment that EMU delay made no sense helped keep the mark subdued. Talk of delay usually boosts the mark as fears recede that it will be replaced by a flimsier single currency.
For dollar/yen, the trade issue took centre stage as the market awaited tonight's data, forecast to show the Japanese surplus grew in May to 549 billion yen from April's 229 billion.
By contrast, data out Thursday are expected to show the U.S. April trade deficit at $10 billion versus $8.5 billion in March.

The market fears this disparity will create tension between the two nations at the G7 summit in Denver on June 20-22, though a Japanese finance ministry official said today that Japan's surplus would not grow enough to invite severe friction.
Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered, said the G7 was unlikely to unleash a volley of exchange rate rhetoric.
"The issue is to try to get Japan to boost demand, and how they do that, rather than by trying to engineer a manipulation of exchange rates," he said.

Ahead of the trade figures, the market was awaiting a swathe of U.S. data today, with the main focus on May consumer prices. Those were expected to support the scenario of subdued inflation suggested by a surprise fall in May PPI announced last week.
The producer price drop poured cold water on speculation that the Federal Reserve would hike interest rates at its next policymaking meeting on July 1-2.
CPI and May housing starts are due at 1230 GMT, with industrial production and capacity utilization out at 1315 GMT, then real earnings at 1400 GMT.
Elsewhere, the mark/yen cross fell to a session low of 65.29 from Monday's European close of 65.63/66 before recovering to 65.49/52 by 1134 GMT.
Traders said the renewed mark/yen buying had helped pull dollar/mark off its highs, especially as an early wave of Swiss franc demand ebbed.
Dollar/Swiss held most of its gains, though, to trade at 1.4470/80 francs at 1134 GMT compared to late yesterday's 1.4397/02. Mark/Swiss climbed to 83.36/41 centimes from 83.27/28.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
